session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men going about everyday life in the UK — making ordinary decisions about food, spending time with friends, navigating work and leisure. The collective identity is grounded in the mundane and the social, not in any ideological or dietary category. This keeps the opening neutral and prevents premature positioning around plant-based eating or gender before participants have found their own footing.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or performative answers. Men may deny gender influence at the level of stated belief while exhibiting it at the level of described behaviour. Needs careful behavioural grounding and readiness to surface contradiction.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): Risk of abstract hypothetical answers that avoid real specificity. Needs probing into concrete, personal barriers — practical, social, emotional — not just general opinion.

Social context of eating with male friends (Sections 1 and 3): The peer-group context is likely to be where gendered food norms operate most visibly. Participants may under-report social pressure; worth watching for indirect references to what 'others' would think.

Making plant-based foods more appealing (Section 5): Risk of group convergence around familiar, safe answers (taste, price, convenience). Need to watch for premature consensus and push for specificity about what would actually shift behaviour, not just attitude.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender: Participants may flatly deny that gender influences their food choices at the stated-attitude level. Use behavioural grounding — ask about specific past moments, not abstract beliefs — especially in Section 3.

Premature consensus on plant-based barriers: Group may converge quickly on taste/price/convenience as the obstacles. Plan a sharpening move for Section 4 or 5 if this happens — e.g., invite someone to speak to a situation where those barriers didn't apply but they still didn't choose plant-based.

Abstract hypothetical drift in Section 4: 'Imagine you decided to go plant-based' may produce wish-list or policy-register answers. Push early for personal and specific: what in their actual life, actual social circle, actual weekly routine would need to shift.

Peer-group conformity pressure within the session itself: A group of men discussing food and masculinity may self-regulate toward conventional masculine positions. Watch for softening of earlier statements and use reflect_contradiction or invite_dissent if this occurs.
Bilal's dietary context: Halal requirements may make the plant-based question land differently. Do not assume or ask; stay alert if he raises it and probe with care if he does.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Light touch. Build rapport, let participants find their voice, do not push for depth. A rich answer in the intro is worth one genuine follow-up but not sustained probing. Section 2: Moderate — behavioural grounding on food decisions, watching for what social and contextual factors participants mention unprompted. Sections 3–5 (main topics): Full probe depth. Push for behavioural specificity, surface contradictions, challenge easy consensus, use invite_dissent if needed. Section 6: Very light — brief open invitation only, do not reopen closed topics unless a participant volunteers something genuinely new.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) weighted most heavily as they carry the research objectives. Context sections (1, 2) given moderate allocation — they warm up and ground the group but should not exhaust the time. Intro and closing are light. Three main topic sections share roughly half the total budget, with Section 3 (gender and food) getting a slight premium as the most likely to require careful probing and contradiction-surfacing.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was introductory — participants oriented themselves geographically and socially, with light banter around travel distances serving as an early bonding mechanism. No substantive themes emerged yet beyond a sense of varied regional backgrounds (Northern Ireland, Yorkshire, South West, Birmingham, London) and a warm, relaxed group tone. The section closed with the first substantive prompt about favourite places to spend time with male friends.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's approach was to establish psychological safety quickly — emphasising no right answers, conversational rather than quiz-like norms, and brief self-introductions to lower stakes. Framing was clear and well-calibrated for an opening. The group responded warmly and without hesitation, suggesting the tone landed well. No intervention was needed to draw out quieter voices at this stage.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the pub as social infrastructure — with a productive urban/rural tension emerging between London's abundance of choice and the 'bedrock' role pubs play in less saturated environments. A secondary theme introduced by Noah added nuance: in Northern Ireland, pubs carry identity and community significance beyond mere practicality. The dominant thread was how place-scarcity shapes social cohesion, with participants interrogating whether forced proximity produces tighter bonds than optionality allows.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening turns developed organically between Connor and Bilal, so the moderator held back to let the urban/rural contrast deepen without intervention. Noah had been silent during a substantively rich exchange, so a direct address was used to draw him in — which succeeded in surfacing the Northern Ireland context and the 'loaded' pub dynamic, a genuinely new thread. The section was closed before that thread could be pursued, which was a trade-off worth flagging.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section established meat-eating as unreflective default across all participants — convenience, habit, and upbringing doing the work rather than conscious choice. A minor but productive tension emerged between Sam's South West provenance-awareness and Noah's corrective: local sourcing in Northern Ireland is inherited routine rather than deliberate values, a useful distinction between cultural food pride and structural habit. Connor remained entirely silent throughout, a participation gap worth monitoring.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator let the dietary baseline establish itself organically before pivoting to the gender question — a reasonable judgment given the section's purpose was scene-setting. The summary-and-redirect move at the close was clean and efficient. The main weakness was not drawing Connor in at any point; four consecutive speakers built a convergent picture without challenge or contrast, which may have narrowed the baseline unnecessarily before the more sensitive gender question.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section surfaced a productive tension between two explanatory frameworks: Noah's argument that meat-eating carries specifically gendered enforcement (vegetarianism reads as soft or feminine, with real social cost), versus Bilal's counter that the mechanism is norm-conformity rather than masculinity per se. Connor moved from scepticism to agreement with Noah; Sam and Henry occupied uncertain middle ground, acknowledging something is 'woven in' without being able to name its precise nature. Regional variation became the section's organising axis.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator let Noah and Connor develop the enforcement/autopilot distinction before widening to the full group — a sound sequencing choice that gave later speakers a developed framework to respond to rather than a blank prompt. Direct addresses to Sam and Henry were well-timed. The closing pivot to the plant-based hypothetical was efficient but slightly abrupt — the Noah/Bilal disagreement about mechanism had genuine depth that could have been held open a little longer before redirecting.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier gender-pressure framework into a more granular question: what actually constitutes a barrier to dietary change? A productive tension emerged between practical inconvenience (dairy, routine, social relationships), the self-policing mechanism of anticipated judgment, and a philosophically sharper question Henry and Connor surfaced — whether preference itself is separable from the pressures that shaped it. Bilal's closing position usefully collapsed that distinction: shaped preferences are still real preferences.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator let the Sam/Noah exchange develop without interruption, then amplified Sam's 'making a statement' formulation to draw the group in — which successfully opened space for Henry and Connor's more structural contributions. Direct addresses to Bilal and Connor were well-timed and drew out the section's sharpest ideas. The transition pivot away from the Henry/Connor debate about preference-formation felt slightly premature; that thread had genuine remaining depth, though the section objective was met.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened the earlier preference-formation debate into a regional spectrum: Connor and Henry converged on the view that normalisation could render plant-based eating invisible by dissolving the conditions that shape preference itself. Noah, Sam, and — more hesitantly — Bilal and Henry pushed back: masculinity norms are structural enough that shifting the food landscape alone won't dissolve them. The section's organising tension was between contextual and structural accounts of why gendered food norms persist.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator let Connor and Henry's philosophical exchange develop before redirecting to the regional voices, which successfully surfaced the London/elsewhere contrast as the section's backbone. Direct addresses to Bilal and Sam after Noah's intervention drew out the gradient rather than a binary split — a productive outcome. The closing summary was accurate and efficient, though the Connor/Henry preference-formation thread was cut slightly early again; that pattern across two sections suggests a recurring trade-off worth watching.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section produced a rare moment of live position-revision: Connor's challenge to the structural account prompted Sam to publicly question his own fatalism, softening the contextual/structural binary that had organised prior sections. The residual tension — whether removing social reaction would be sufficient or whether something persists underneath — was left productively unresolved, suggesting participants left with genuinely updated rather than merely performed positions.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section was brief and moderator-light by design — a closing invitation rather than a substantive probe. Reflecting Connor's formulation back before opening the floor gave it weight without crowding the closing space. Sam's voluntary revision suggested that framing landed. The main trade-off was speed: the Connor/Sam exchange had remaining depth, but session time was exhausted and forcing more would have felt extractive rather than genuine.

I'm not looking for particular views, and I'm not trying to nudge you anywhere — I'm just curious about your actual experiences and opinions, whatever those are. So try not to overthink things, just speak freely. And this is meant to feel like a conversation, not a quiz — so if something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in. Okay — let's start simply. If you could each just say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that would be great.
Yeah, hi. I'm Henry. I'm from Birmingham, so not far to come today really — just across the city. Cheers for having us.

Yeah, hi. I'm Connor. I'm from London — well, Greater London — so I'm already here, which is handy. Bit different from having to trek across the country like some of you probably have. Cheers for organizing this.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Noah. I'm from Northern Ireland, so bit more of a journey than you lot, to be honest — flew in this morning. Suburban area just outside Belfast. But yeah, good to be here.
Yeah, hi. I'm Bilal. I'm from Yorkshire — urban area in Yorkshire and the Humber. So bit of a drive down, but nothing too mad. Thanks for having me as well.

But if I'm being honest, it comes down to pubs most of the time — there's a few decent ones near me where you can actually sit down and talk without it being too loud, you know? That matters more as you get a bit older, I think. When you're younger it's all about the nightlife and the noise, but now it's more just... you want somewhere you can have a proper conversation with your mates.

There's also the local park if the weather's decent — bit of a walk, grab a coffee, maybe kick a ball around if we're feeling it. But honestly, a lot of the time it's just someone's house, isn't it? Stick the football on, have some food, that's easy. Less hassle than trying to book anywhere or deal with the whole night out thing. London's got loads of options, but yeah, the pubs are the go-to really.

If you're meeting someone, that's where you go.

I think Connor's right that you want somewhere you can actually talk — that matters. But in a lot of places around where I am, the pub's almost the only real social infrastructure you've got, if I'm honest. It's not that there's loads of options like in London. It's just the default because it's there and it's reliable.

House hangs are good too, obviously. But yeah, I'd say the pub's probably where I spend most time with the lads. Get some food, watch a match, whatever. It's just... it's easy and it's the thing, isn't it?

But what you're saying about the pub being kind of the backbone of things, the reliable thing that's just always there... that's different, isn't it? 

I mean, we've got loads of pubs here too, obviously, but there's also gyms, clubs, cinemas, whatever — so you're kind of spoiled for choice in a way that maybe masks what's actually happening. Whereas it sounds like what you're describing is the pub being the actual social glue, you know? The thing that actually holds people together because it's genuinely the place where people congregate.

I suppose that does make a difference to how you experience it. It's not just one option among many — it's kind of the bedrock. That's actually quite interesting.

Like, when there's infinite options, you're shopping around for the best experience or whatever. But when it's the pub, it's just... it's where your mates are. It's where you know people will be on a Friday night. It's not aspirational, it's just practical.

I reckon that does shape things. Like how tight-knit you are, maybe. Because you're forced into proximity in a way, not because you've all chosen the same trendy spot, but because it's just the thing. Does that make sense? I'm not saying it's better or worse, but it's definitely different.
